My mother's restaurant has nine tables, one oven and no dishwasher except me.

On Saturdays I work from 4:30 p.m. until the last pan is dry, which is usually around 11. Nobody would call it glamorous work—my hands smell like lemon soap for two days afterward—but it is where I learned to count. Not arithmetic: counting. How many plates are out, how many are coming back, how long until table six needs forks.

A well-run kitchen is a prediction that keeps coming true. When it stops coming true, you find out in about ninety seconds, and so does everyone else.

I'm applying to study operations research because I want to know whether the thing I do by feel at the sink can be written down. I suspect it can. I also suspect the written-down version will be worse than my mother's, who has never written anything down in her life and has never once run out of forks.
